title: From Threat Detection to Decision Rights: Evidence-Constrained Cyber-Threat Intelligence and Accountable Agentic AI
content: Large  language models (LLMs) can help cyber-threat-intelligence (CTI) teams interpret unstructured reports, identify potential techniques, and draft response recommendations. The existence of a plausible narrative, however, is not evidence that the threat attribution is warranted or that an automated action is authorised. This conceptual article proposes an evidence-constrained and intervention-ready architecture for LLM-assisted CTI. It develops a bounded critical synthesis of recent research on LLM-assisted CTI and cloud retrieval, established cybersecurity standards, and recent work on action-level accountability. The model passes every interpretation through five gates: source admission, claim extraction, interpretation, decision authorisation, and execution with post-incident review. It specifies a claim-to-evidence ledger, attack-taxonomy version tracking, a calibrated abstention rule, an approval ladder for consequential actions, and a privacy-sensitive audit record. Three hypothetical scenarios (a contaminated threat report, false corroboration across copied sources, and an over-confident automated quarantine) show how a system might fail despite strong benchmark performance. The paper offers evaluation criteria covering support fidelity, mapping accuracy, adversarial robustness, escalation quality, and the time needed to reconstruct and reverse harmful actions. It makes no claim to have trained, deployed, or benchmarked a new CTI model. Its principal contribution is to reframe trustworthy CTI as a question of decision rights: not only whether an AI system recognises a threat, but who may rely on its interpretation, who can authorise an intervention, and who can challenge a damaging classification.
